speechtext:
In rising to speak on farm credit I feel that there are substantial areas, particularly in respect of the Farm Credit Corporation, that deserve wide scrutiny at this point. Since the original Farm Credit Act was instituted there has been a substantial change in farm economics, marketing problems and in the general economic climate in which the farm industry must operate. During these past ten years there has been a phenomenal increase in the price of land, in the price of machinery and farm operating costs. The increase in land price has been aided by the rapid rate of inflation, competition from would-be new farmers, and competition by established farmers who increase their holdings when the amount of land available remains static. There is just no more land being created. As well, there has been
762	COMMONS
Farm Improvement Loans Act some demand by investors as a hedge against inflation. All this has increased the amount of capital required to carry on a viable farm operation so that the capital required is now in the neighbourhood of $60,000 to $100,000 for a modest farm.
So far as farm improvement loans are concerned, in respect of which the banks and other companies will be lending money, it would seem that the rate of interest on money should be tied to the prime interest rate. This would introduce a flexibility into the lending which I think would be very advantageous and would prevent a situation that has occurred in the past few months.
In relation to the Farm Credit Act I should like to point out that the amount of farm capitalization necessary to carry on an adequate farm is of a large order. The capital repayment necessary to pay for a farm involving a $60,000 to $100,000 capital investment is in the nature of $3,000 to $5,000 per year. This is a very heavy burden for the farmers to bear in relation to their earnings. With the high level of income tax this means that the farmers' standard of living is seriously compromised. He is placed at a serious disadvantage in respect of his living standards, compared with his counterpart in the city who has the advantage of having the necessary capital supplied by others. In discussing with young farmers the reason they leave the farm for relatively low wage jobs in the city, this would appear to be a factor.
Although it is not usually recognized as such, in our high cost economy, the old adage that the farmer lives poor and dies rich will be much more applicable in future than it is at present. It would seem obvious that, in the future, capital repayment on land for farms by the individual farmer will have to be spread out over long periods. Indeed it will be likely that in his lifetime a farmer will not often retire the debt acquired in the purchase of land and the building of his farm unit. In order to retain the family farm unit it will be necessary to allow the accumulation of capital by a farmer and his family to some greater degree than is allowed under our present taxation structure. This would require the calling of witnesses before a committee to study thoroughly the agricultural field, the lending field and the taxation field. A means must be found by which the farmer will be in a position to retain more of the capital he has accumulated, particularly in view of the very high income tax level. Some thought should be given to a program which would allow a

DEBATES	October 3, 1968
farm to be passed from generation to generation without complete refinancing. I notice a change in the resolution which might have been incorporated for the purpose and, if so, I welcome it as a useful instrument.
A small farm has now become a small business the operation of which requires a major effort on the part of the farmer. The business of lending money should be considered in the light of the fact that the individual farmer is a businessman generally alone, and that therefore our present taxation and social structure, as in the case of a small business, does not give the farmer a proper opportunity to take his place in society. If the family farmer does disappear in the foreseeable future his demise will be caused by the taxation policies in relation to business. At the present time the family farm, on the whole, is efficient and provides more food more cheaply than does any corporation. However the family farm must be allowed to operate and breathe; otherwise it will be taken over by corporation farms to the disadvantage of the whole community. The Farm Credit Corporation has been established now for a long time, but in view of the great changes and a whole host of new problems that have arisen it should be studied in depth.
The only way to achieve this is for the agricultural committee to carry out a study in depth of this problem. Until this is done the interest rate should not change from its present level of 5 per cent and should not be subject to change by the governor in council operating in secrecy and without accountability. The farmer must know what his interest rate is to be. There should be no doubt on his part concerning the interest rate. An interest rate of 5 per cent is reasonable on the average over a long period. Although the funds for lending by the Farm Credit Corporation are taken out of the consolidated revenue fund, much money has already been paid back into the fund, so that to some extent it is self-sustaining. No change should be made in the interest rate or in the terms of interest until there has been a review of the necessity for this, and of the other factors involved in a study of the interest rate.
It might be that the Farm Credit Corporation has funds of its own which it could use for the purpose of carrying on modest research. It might be reasonable that a young farmer could be given a rate of interest lower than the normal rate for a period of time, until he becomes established and is in a position to pay a higher interest rate. Farm credit is a very important factor in the business of
October 3, 1968

farming. In considering the problems which face farmers today it is on a par with marketing. It is absolutely essential that a good system of farm loans be evolved and that changes be made to meet varying conditions. There must be greater means by which farm credit can be obtained. These bills seem to be merely a hurried extension of existing legislation, and do not indicate that there has been thoughtful consideration of the needs of the farmer.

It is not only the bills referred to in these resolutions which are being held up, but there are other important bills waiting in the wings, such as the bill concerning the increase in cash advances. Much of the debate so far has been more or less irrelevant, and certainly it has been time consuming and repetitive. I am afraid that a good deal of it will be repeated when we discuss the bill in the house later.
What are we supposed to be doing here? I believe we are supposed to be discussing three resolutions which deal with programs which have been in operation for some years, and which have been accepted and used by the farmers of Canada. We should be discussing the renewal of the Farm Improvement Loans Act, revisions to the Farm Credit Act and revisions to the Farm Machinery Syndicates Credit Act. But we seem to be ranging very far from these topics at times.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
In regard to the Farm Improvement Loans Act, I think it is important to reactivate this as soon as possible, because many farmers are waiting for these loans. I do not think it is particularly beneficial to farmers to have us spending time trying to assess blame, or take credit for things done or left undone in the past years or months. I think it is important to get these bills introduced and passed. The farmers are waiting for this legislation in order to make use of these provisions.
I am very pleased to hear that credit unions are to be allowed to become lending

Farm Improvement Loans Act institutions under this act. The provisions which make it possible for farmers to borrow money under the act to purchase small land holdings over a relatively brief period of time will be beneficial as well.
I want to say a few words about the Farm Credit Act and the farm syndicate loans act. Farmers have accepted the provisions of these acts, and they have accomplished at least two beneficial results. They have made it possible for farmers to attain economic units, and have created a great deal of efficiency in farm units in Canada. They have also made it possible to transfer farms to the younger generation, and this is one of the most important things that can be done at this time.
The proposal to increase the capital under this act will enable a continuing use of these funds in future years. I believe also that the father-son partnership provision is good. It will enable such a partnership to borrow more money than might otherwise be available.
I welcome also the provision which makes credit available to farm co-operatives and farm corporations under the Farm Credit Corporation. I think it is a good idea that the people living on Indian reserves, either in bands or as individuals, will now be allowed, once this resolution becomes law, to borrow money from the Farm Credit Corporation.
There is one reservation I have in respect of this resolution regarding the Farm Credit Corporation act. I sympathize with many of the members who have expressed their concern, particularly those members on the opposition benches. I made a similar statement during the debate in reply to the speech from the throne that I should like to see interest rates remain the same as they are at present under the Farm Credit Corporation act.

Hear, hear.
I am not sure that I will be successful in persuading my colleagues on this side of the house to support my stand in this matter, but if anyone can do this it is not likely to be someone on the opposition side. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my only reason for speaking on this resolution this evening is my concern about its implications. I am of a different opinion from the hon. mem-
October 3, 1968

Farm Improvement Loans Act ber for Assiniboia, who suggested there was nothing to worry about. The resolution we have before us should be considered seriously.
I agree with another hon. member who suggested that interest rates on these loans should be pegged. I am particularly concerned with interest rates because of what happened many years ago. I remember the hardships that my family suffered when trying to keep up the payments on loans, due to interest rates. They had to obtain a mortgage in order to stay in business. In 1937 the bank which held the mortgage on the land my father owned in Alberta required him to sell the cattle he had to stay in business. I remember their taking the machinery and the land, and everything else it was possible to remove in order to pay up the mortgage. These people were not interested in my father keeping his farm lands. It is my suggestion tonight that if we permit this resolution to pass in its present form, without pegging the interest rate, we can expect the same thing to happen again.
Surely no one questions the fact that the Farm Improvement Loans Act should be reinstated; but these changes, whether acceptable or not, should not be shoved down our throats. We must seriously consider the interest rates which are spelled out in respect of guaranteed farm improvement loans prescribed by the governor in council. We are all aware of the fact that the N.H.A. rates are those prescribed by the governor in council.
When we look at the situation which exists throughout Canada we realize that only those people who earn $8,000 a year can qualify for these loans. If this measure is passed in its present form, the farmers who are not earning that amount of money could be in the same position as 80 per cent of the people in this country who cannot qualify for an N.H.A. loan. I hope the minister will realize that the young people and the elderly people who must obtain loans under the act are the people who are most important to this industry. Having regard to the analogy I have made, we are making provisions to allow the governor in council to practise discrimination against the farming people of this country.
The Minister of Agriculture said, on September 30, that the Minister of Finance advised that when the legislation was introduced in the house the new lending period would be made retroactive from July 1, having regard to loans made after June 30, and that these would be guaranteed by the government. I ask members of the house what

better lending institution could possibly be found than the government of this country. I am sure anyone who wanted to establish a lending institution would be pleased to know that the loans he was making were backed by the people of Canada. The Minister of Agriculture suggested it was important to keep in mind that the object of this legisla-ion is to facilitate guaranteed loans to farmers, but the ultimate decision of whether such loans are made rests with the lender.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
These facts will help to throw some light on what has been taking place in this country ever since the war. The defenders of the profit, or free enterprise system, have been taking their prosperity in cash, while the ordinary John Doe has been encouraged to take his prosperity on credit. I suggest this is exactly what is happening today. This was offered as a remedy for his own tight money problem, resulting from too much money being drained out of the economy in profits. This stimulant could have only temporary benefits and the sources were limited.
As the economy has slowed down, the government has been unable or unwilling to diagnose the case or come to grips with realities. Instead they are experimenting with various kinds of free enterprise nostrums. They have cut taxes for the rich. When this did not produce the desired results, they increased taxes but provided refunds to corporations, which simply means that the corporations were not taxed at all.
Those who have taken $5 billion out of the economy in 12 short months are the people who receive special consideration at the hands of the old line parties. Having drained the public purse, they now favour high interest rates for money. I include both the Liberals and the Conservatives in these remarks. I do not think there is any question whatsoever that there is not one iota of difference between the Liberals and the Conservatives, with regard to protecting the private corporate interest in this country. I appreciate the position the Conservatives have taken in this particular situation, but I wonder what they would do if they were now in office.
There is one more analogy I should like to make, Mr. Chairman. It is that many, many people are very critical of the hippies that we have in Canada today. So far as the hippies are concerned, I believe they are fed up to the teeth with the absolute inactivity of the government of Canada. I am sure they are fed up to the teeth with the absolute lack of
Ociober 3, 1968

responsibility on the part of members of parliament, when they fail to meet the issues head on. In this regard I refer to the resolution now before us. Here we are giving the right to raise the interest rate on farm improvement loans to the economic hippies- and I am sure this country is full of economic hippies. We do not have to look very far to realize this and to realize they do not care what really happens to the farmer today.
The most important fact we have to face today is that farm people very much need the money that is available to them by way of a farm improvement loan. I assure the committee that the people to whom I have spoken are most desirous of being able to avail themselves of farm improvement loans, but they are not desirous of availing themselves of such loans if there is an increase in the interest rate. These remarks apply to the people with whom I have spoken within the last week, and before that. They suggested that, because of the present interest rate they are unable at this time to take advantage of the loans available to them. I am sure that when the bill following this resolution is passed there will be absolutely no way of pegging the interest rate.

I think what happened this afternoon is a perfect example of what happens with this government. The minister neglected to give us information on the measures proposed in the order paper, but the information was given to the press ahead of time. I realize that resolution No. 5 contains many necessary provisions. It has always been my opinion that the government should recognize there are experts in every field with which they deal. These experts are not necessarily in the ranks of the government. I believe that every government should at least recognize the fact that there must be consultation with those people most directly affected by the legislation proposed, and I suggest the people in the agricultural
Farm Improvement Loans Act field should be consulted about these matters. People representing farm organizations should be given the opportunity to discuss the matters with which we are now dealing.
One hon. member suggested that a royal commission be appointed to study this whole question. I have absolutely no confidence in royal commissions. I suggest that the only way to enact the best kind of legislation to solve these problems is to consult the people concerned. 1 agree that this discussion must come to an end. Many of the things that have been said are being repeated. I do not mean just the western farmers, but the farmers in this whole nation. First of all I want to congratulate the last speaker upon some of the cogent remarks he made on the matter of increasing the interest rate. One of the things we must keep in mind is that the field of agriculture has changed a great deal in the last 70 years. It has changed from a farmer providing food for himself and another person in 1900, to today providing food for upwards of 35 people. This shows the great scientific developments that have been made in farming. As a matter of fact, I do not think any industry in Canada has produced, per capita, the increased rate of production of the farm operator.
This proves that the farm operator has the necessary skill, the necessary education and the know-how to run his farm, given the opportunity to obtain capital. Another fact we must keep in mind is that farming is a costly

Farm Improvement Loans Act business. You can start an operation with a dairy farm and buy 25 or 30 cows, and you will pay upwards of $300 to $500 per cow. Then you have to buy coolers and all the other things that go with operating a dairy farm. You also have to pay high wages for any help you employ. Particularly in dairying. This can be multiplied many times over, on bigger operations but it shows the capital that is necessary to run a farm, increasing with the size.

If there is to be such a high rate of interest, then it would not pay the man to start farming because it would be very difficult nowadays to start a dairy farm of 100 acres fully equipped for under $80,000. At 7 or 8 per cent the interest on that would be about $6,000 a year, before there was any income whatsoever. This is one thing we have to keep in mind. On the one hand there is the high value of investment in this industry, and on the other hand we subsidize the automobile manufacturers up to $50 million a year, and with no qualms at all. The Canadian people have the right to subsidize farming operations because when we look at the facts and figures we find that there are no other people in the world who are as cheaply fed, with the possible exception of those in the country to the south, the U.S.A. as are the Canadian people. We also find that in relation to their income, the money which Canadians spend on food is less per capita, according to their earning power-with one exception, the United States

than anywhere else in the world.
So we do not need to apologize for subsidizing this industry. As a matter of fact, if we do not make it possible for the young fellow to start a farming operation, we may have to pay the penalty of paying through the nose because we will not have his products to sell or the food to buy to eat. Last year we imported into this country some $300 million worth of goods which we could produce right here in Canada, and our total imports of agricultural products ran upwards of $900 million. These are facts which we should consider very seriously in this house. Here we have an industry producing cheaper than anywhere in the world, with one exception, but we quibble with them and say they have to pay an interest rate which is sometimes as high as 8 to 10 per cent. This does not make common sense. This is one industry which it would pay to subsidize, because food is a necessity. We have to have it. I do not

see why any apology should be made for keeping the rate at a level which the farmer can afford.
As I said before, we have to consider the farmer's high cost of investment. Who can start a farm of 100 acres and invest $80,000 in a dairy herd, and at the same time borrow a sufficient amount of money to purchase the equipment necessary to run it at the proposed rate, and make it a paying proposition.
The second point I wish to make is that the farmer is not only a producer but also a purchaser. He purchases the farm equipment that is manufactured in some city which employs labour. If this factory is not selling its products, it does not employ labour, the result is unemployment and the unemployed will have to be given assistance. We have here a two edged sword. The farmer of today is a specialist in his own right. If he is in the dairy business, he produces milk. If he is in the hog business, he produces hogs. However, that farmer does not generally produce more than one product. Many of them do not even have their own garden produce. They go to the store to buy it, just like the fellow in town. However, let us compare the farmer with the city dweller who purchases his food and shelter. He does the same as the farmer, but the farmer is also producing goods and he needs equipment which is manufactured in that town or city.
So let us not apologize. Anyone here who will stand up and apologize for helping the farmer is not thinking in the right way, or has not looked at the other side of the picture. He has not considered what the farmers are doing for this country. As a matter of fact, I think the hon. member for Timiskam-ing stated that the total administration cost amounted to only $3 million out of $263 million. We wonder about the economic pattern of this government, but apparently the clouds are being blown away and a distinct pattern is now emerging. On five separate items, the Canada student loans, the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the Farm Machinery Syndicates Credit Act, and, if you look down a little further, the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, the government has now revealed what we may come to expect as government policy in regard to various federal assistance programs.
Two tendencies appear clear: First, that at this time the government is no longer prepared to keep the interest rates stable and to keep them down to the previous lending levels and, second, that private lending agencies such as trusts, banks and mortgage companies as well as credit unions and caisses populates, will be the major suppliers of assistance funds, but at increased rates, which will encourage them to open their purses once more to help the country-banks, trusts and mortgage companies being the loyal corporate citizens that they are.

All of us know what happened to the National Housing Act rates during recent months. Skyrocketting interest
Farm Improvement Loans Act rates put the purchase of a new home hopelessly beyond the reach of the average Canadian. Similar flexibility is being planned for at least five other assistance programs which I have mentioned.
The first inkling of what was to come was the announcement on August 16 made by the Minister of Finance that henceforth the Canada student loan rate will no longer be five and three quarters per cent but will be pegged at 1 per cent above the bond yield on August 16 of every year. This effectively put the summer work-short college students further in hock than ever. What I am asking the minister through you, Mr. Chairman, is this: What will the situation be as a result of this proposed legislation when we come to consider the farmers?
We will soon have before us for amendment and renewal three agricultural assistance bills. We have the Farm Improvement Loans Act, which is an intermediate term program of five to ten years for the purchase of equipment and machinery. This will allow money to be made available through banks at 5 per cent interest rates. We also have the Farm Credit Act which was for land purchases mainly and is now to be broadened. Of course, this is going to fill the demand for longer term loans, that is between 25 and 29 years.

Now, Mr. Chairman, probably the most important amendment proposed is the one which, instead of fixing interest rates on these loans, would permit the rate henceforth to be set by the governor in council. If the proposed measures are brought forward and passed we will no longer be dealing with the same legislation.
I was not sent to Ottawa to sit idly by while some of these provisions were made into law, without speaking on behalf of my constituents and the other people of this country. I see in this resolution the wording:
-to substitute for the 5 per cent rate of interest on guaranteed farm improvement loans made under the act such rate or rates of interest as may be prescribed by the governor in council;-
I do not intend to stand by idly. It is no wonder that the banks would like to lend less money to farmers as a result of the increase allowed in bank interest rates before this parliament was

convened. The government must accept the responsibility for this situation, but what is it doing? The government is now looking to the farmer, the fishermen, the home owners and the students of this country to pay the whole shot. We could argue that perhaps some of the facts suggested by the Economic Council should be modified, but there is one conclusion that cannot be doubted. The productivity of the agricultural industry must be increased. That industry needs more capital. It would be a sound policy on the part of the government to peg the interest rates that the farmers of this country must pay.
The fact is well known that if the farmers have to pay high interest rates, and if there is no reduction in that rate as a result of this legislation, their production costs will be much higher than they can afford. The returns the farmer receives from his production are too low as compared with the interest rate he must pay. The minister has suggested that by this proposed legislation the government is helping the agricultural industry. This is not a measure which will help. If the government wants to help assure a sound and stable agricultural economy, it should reconsider this plan and introduce a fixed reasonable interest rate, such as the 5 per cent interest rate which has been in existence up to this time.

Farm Improvement Loans Act
One of the greatest problems facing the Ontario farmers in my area today is the inability to obtain sufficient funds to purchase the necessary equipment required for the successful production and harvesting of corn. One of the problems is caused by the deterioration in the marketing of corn, which is of such an extent that farmers are turning to other sources of income with which to buy machinery. The cost of machinery used in the growing and harvesting of corn is very great because the machinery is of a very specialized nature. The cost of this machinery is somewhat higher than that used in the production and harvesting of other grain crops.

The machinery companies are taking full advantage of this as businessmen, which they are, but they seem to be charging exorbitant interest rates compared with those formerly applicable in respect of a farm syndicate or a farm improvement loan.

I hope that in his address tomorrow the Minister of Agriculture will indicate to the farmers that they will not be needing this extra money in the form of loans, that they need not be concerned about an increase in interest rates, that the policy of the government will be flexible enough to stabilize the market, thus putting the farmer in a position to finance his own equipment. This is all the farmers of this country are asking for. This is all they are asking for in connection with farm improvement and farm syndicate loans. They consider these loans as an emergency measure to tide them over this very critical period in corn growing and marketing in southwestern Ontario. This money is required because their costs are increasing month by month and year by year.
I hope the minister and his colleagues on that side of the house are not in a position to understand that the matter is of a critical nature, that there is great concern for the harvest this year, that what the farmers receive from that harvest will in great measure influence the amount of money they will need by way of a farm improvement or farm syndicate loan. It will indeed influence how much money farmers will be seeking from the Farm Credit Corporation to increase their holdings.
I hope, Mr. Chairman, that because of these few remarks you have appreciated that corn has a definite bearing on the resolutions with which we are dealing tonight. I trust Your Honour appreciates that there is a close connection between the two. The matter is in the minister's hands and I am sure he will deal with it in detail tomorrow.

Mr. Chairman, I can understand the hon. member's desire to receive answers to all these questions, and I will answer as many of them as I can. First of all, the rates under the Farm Machinery Syndicates Credit Act are not limited by statute now. They are what are called economic rates, that is a rate which is 1 per cent above what the farm credit corporation pays for the money. There is no intention to change the rates now in existence.
So far as the limits are concerned, it would be far easier if I could deal with this matter when the bill is before the house, and I certainly will. It is not intended to raise the limits appreciably. However, what we are more concerned about, with the limited experience we have now with the farm machinery syndicates bill, is that we would like to change the structure of the entity. Up to now a group of farmers had to form a separate entity or a syndicate, and had to have an agreement. If they were in some kind of a corporation or co-operative, previously this did not satisfy the terms of the act; but now we see no reason, on the basis of our experience, to require them to set up a separate agreement if they already have one.
Second, we believe that buildings which can be used by more than one farmer should come within the scope of the act. This
Farm Machinery Syndicates Credit Act includes the site for the buildings, and other things that can be used by more than one farmer. This was the purpose of the Farm Machinery Syndicates Credit Act in the first place. Now we find there are some rules, regulations and statutory limitations which should really be changed in view of the experience which was gained. However, I would ask hon. members to allow me to deal with these specific questions when the bill comes up for discussion. We have it ready and we will bring it in as soon as the resolution is passed. I wish to say sincerely to hon. members that I will be able to deal with these questions much more effectively at that stage.

maintopic: CONSUMER AFFAIRS-DANGER ARISING FROM DISPOSABLE BOTTLES
CONSUMER AFFAIRS-DANGER ARISING FROM DISPOSABLE BOTTLES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in raising the question I did the other day concerning disposable bottles and the responsibility of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs to the public in this regard, I believe I am raising an important question

with considerable implication to our society. I am pleased to see that the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz), the parliamentary secretary to the minister, is in the house tonight and will be able to convey to the minister some of the arguments I put forward. I urge the minister in this particular case, as he will be urged in other cases, to be the ombudsman for the people and to represent the interests of the public against particular interests in our society.
If there is to be any meaning in the euphonic passage in the speech from the throne, the government can prove it at this point. I may just recall to the house that passage which said that-
-facilities for the repose of the mind and restoration of the spirit, for sport, and for physical relaxation are and will be of increasing importance to our social environment.
I suggest that unless some action is taken with regard to disposable bottles, which are becoming a curse in our society, there will be very little repose of the mind or of the spirit in our society. These words in the speech from the throne will be hollow and mocking.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
The two newspapers in the Waterloo riding have reported on the situation. I should like to quote from the Evening Reporter of July 25 in which there is an article which reads:
If some type of action isn't taken soon, it could not longer be safe to walk barefoot in the park or on the beaches along Puslinch Lake because of broken glass and discarded tin cans.
And each morning, patrols of Hespeler's board of works visit town playgrounds and parks to pick up the shards and slivers of glass.
In the Kitchener-Waterloo Record there is an article which reads:
The program is acute in city recreation areas. It will become acute in rural areas. The bottles are finding their way into pasturefields from roadside. They shatter on contact producing slivers and shards of glass.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, these bottles are becoming a menace to man and beasts alike. The idea of the barefoot boy, so revered in our history and ideology, may very well be a thing of the past. Many public bodies have condemned the use of disposable bottles and I should like particularly to congratulate the city of Kitchener which passed a resolution calling on other municipalities to outlaw their use. This resolution has received a great deal of support from such organizations as the Canadian School Trustees Association, which met in Ottawa; the Ontario Parks Association, which met at
October 3, 1968

Brantford and the Ontario Mayors and Reeves Association. The last named organization has supported this position for several years.
In fairness I might point out that, to my knowledge, only one municipality, Etobicoke, has opposed this resolution. It should not come as any surprise that the largest manufacturer of disposable bottles is located in that area. The companies making these bottles will argue that they are not the only ones creating problems of pollution or danger to the public. This is probably true. They are not the only ones, but they are one of the significant ones. If it is any satisfaction to them, I think they should be aware that in the battle to clean up our environment and make it more safe, they will not be the only ones on whom attention will be focused.
It is often said-and the disposable bottle people have said it-that, after all, they only produce these things to meet customer demands. I cannot recall staying up nights hoping and wishing that somebody would invent a disposable bottle I could use, nor can I recall many consumers who have. I feel this is one further example of corporate groups in our society promoting and marketing products, not so much because they benefit the public but because they happen to benefit the particular interests concerned.
In this case, I feel we have to distinguish clearly between the interests of the consumer and the interests of private corporations. I believe that those who have foisted this disposable bottle upon the public have done the public a great disservice. I think it is an example of commercial irresponsibility and a piece of arrogance, especially when they say they are producing them to meet consumer demand. To the profit oriented or the lazy in our society, these bottles may be a blessing; but to others who want to clean up our environment, who feel there are higher social priorities, disposable bottles are becoming a curse. It is the classic struggle between private good and public benefit and I hope the consumer department will look after the interests of the public.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Haidasz (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
maintopic: CONSUMER AFFAIRS-DANGER ARISING FROM DISPOSABLE BOTTLES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in so far as the nonreturnable bottles are concerned, and especially the problem that they create in our communities, I join with the hon. member in deploring the situation. The minister's office has informed me that some time ago they received a resolution passed by the legislature
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion of Alberta asking the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs to study and consider the problem created by non-returnable bottles. Since my minister assumed office he has had a number of meetings with his officials on this question, and there appears to be some difficulty in determining the jurisdiction of the department with regard to this problem.
While already there is legislation and some regulations in force dealing with the packaging of food and medicines to ensure purity, and while we in the department are contemplating legislation to deal with the prohibition or regulation of the sale of hazardous products, non-returnable bottles would not appear to fall within either category.
However, Mr. Speaker, in line with the minister's duty to promote and encourage the institution of practices tending to improve protection of the Canadian consumer and to co-operate with provincial governments or their agencies, or with private groups, the minister will be having further talks with his officials and will consider the question of nonreturnable bottles, with a view to formulating some type of regulation.
After these departmental talks, it is intended to invite representatives of the manufacturers, the users and the retail distributors of these bottles to Ottawa to discuss the problems and all proposals, as well as to ascertain from these people what they intend to do relative to the problem mentioned by the hon. member.

maintopic: EDUCATION-AGREEMENT ON GRADE AND SUBJECT STANDARDS
EDUCATION-AGREEMENT ON GRADE AND SUBJECT STANDARDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope that I can survive these few moments on my feet without being ruled out of order. This will be a rare if not unique experience for me.
About a week ago, Mr. Speaker, I asked the following question which I directed at the time to the Secretary of State, as reported at page 469 of Hansard:
In view of the Canadian School Trustees' recent resolution calling for more uniform education standards across Canada, will the minister give consideration to establishing a national office of education to provide leadership for greater interprovincial agreement on grade and subject standards for Canadian schools?
Now, Mr. Speaker, in asking this question I am bound to go beyond the immediate terms of the question before us; for while greater interprovincial agreement on grade and subject standards might occur, and possibly
October 3, 1968

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion already has occurred, without the establishment of a national office of education, perhaps progress toward this end will surely be more rapid under the auspices of such an office.
Certainly there are many education professionals who would disagree with the need for uniformity-and indeed, fear the effects of it-if the term uniformity is taken to mean complete congruency of grade, subject and textbook adoption from one end of the land to the other. I would include myself among those who would be against the establishment of a national office of education if I felt that its inauguration would hobble any imaginative or innovative approach to publicly supported learning.
Uniformity, you see, can only go so far, because an overdose can be stifling and deadly, whether it is within one school, within one province or across a whole nation. Public education historically has been preoccupied with group learning and the supposed efficiency intended to result from improved class or mass methods and techniques. But the results of such preoccupation has been almost uniformly disappointing. That groups learn anything is a misconception, and within this misconception lies the root of the problem. Groups learn nothing. Only individuals are capable of learning, and he, the individual, has often been overlooked by the education industry.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
In the long run, Mr. Speaker, what we need is not greater uniformity in our curricular offerings to young people, but more, much more, provision for the multiplicity of talents, Interests and needs of each individual student. Just as a hungry man does not want a meal in the long run but immediately, so does the need for more interprovincial agreement on educational standards become, in the short run, an extremely desirable objective. I have little doubt that a national office of education could assist us here.
Certainly, it seems that since our people move about the country from province to province a great deal now, grade 7 in British Columbia should be similar to grade 7 in Ontario. Where does this paucity of educational consensus leave the migrant's child? Course offerings differ widely from grade to grade, and from province to province, with richer provinces and regions in Canada providing enriching optional subjects, and better qualified teachers and the disadvantaged

regions tending to be as impoverished in educational opportunities as they are in other ways.
The 13 years of secondary school required by Ontario, for instance, in contrast to the 12 years required in British Columbia, discouraged me from bringing my family to Ottawa this session, since one of my children would face an extra year's schooling here before graduation and the beginning of professional training. Wide provincial variations in university entrance requirements also exist and could benefit from rationalization. I think I have said enough to highlight the educational hodgepodge that already exists in Canada.
A standing committee of ministers of education was established in 1966; there was hope of forming a secretariat in Ottawa; but plans for that seem to have been curtailed. One official of a national educational association commented that it seems to take the council of ministers six months to make one breast stroke. Indeed, a breast stroke, however leisurely, is progress of a sort for provincial representatives who hitherto disdained to get their feet wet in national problems. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the establishment of a national office of education under the Secretary of State is necessary in order to bring into focus possible solutions to national educational problems which might otherwise languish for years before ad hoc committees of ministers or Canadian education association officials.
I see a national office of education primarily as a co-ordinating body to provide leadership, or a centre, if you like, which would say to the rest of Canada and the world that our national government regards education as one of the most important functions of national endeavour. A national office must be more than a symbol, because federal support for education is a major budget item each year. I have seen in Hansard for 1966 that amounts ranging from $250 million to $500 million per year were spent as the federal contribution. Yet the federal government's position in its relations with provinces on educational matters is all pay and no say.
The issue is not whether the federal or provincial governments have the say in education or, according to Professor J. Katz of the University of British Columbia, one as to which governments have the right to represent Canada at international conferences on education, but whether Canadians can afford anything but full co-operation between federal
October 3. 1968

and provincial governments on all educational matters at home and abroad.
In the United States, where 50 independent, but similar educational systems exist, as opposed to ten in this country, they found it expedient to establish 101 years ago a national office of education. Can we therefore afford to persist in our leisurely approach?
I close, Mr. Speaker, with a plea that we reform the way we handle educational problems at the national level. To support my plea I quote the words of the Prime Minister, in August of last year who, when he referred to his 1956 writings on Quebec education, wrote:
The consequence was that we had to wait twenty years lor the only reform that really counts: education. 1 agree that reform in education is the only reform that really counts.
It may not be too extravagant to suggest that the structure of education at the national level is roughly equivalent to the irrelevant and unrealistic structure that existed in Quebec 20 years ago in order to prepare the citizens of the province to meet the challenges of the day and the days ahead. The time therefore to establish a national office of education is now.

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Stanbury (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
maintopic: EDUCATION-AGREEMENT ON GRADE AND SUBJECT STANDARDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is aware that the Canadian council of ministers of education was created in September 1967. Its purpose is, and I quote:
-to allow the ministers to have consultation on matters of common interest and to allow full cooperation between provincial governments in common fields of interest in education. The council will co-operate with other educational organizations to promote education in Canada.
The permanent structure of the secretariat and the scope of its field of action are not yet known. Still, the secretariat should serve not only as an instrument for consultation and as the framework for common activity but it should also facilitate agreement on the main points of general policy.
The member may rest assured that the federal government is at the complete disposal of the provincial governments to achieve their objectives in that field.

maintopic: HARBOURS-ROBERTS BANK, B.C.-REPRESENTATIONS RESPECTING RAIL LINE
HARBOURS-ROBERTS BANK, B.C.-REPRESENTATIONS RESPECTING RAIL LINE
speechtext:
During the sitting of the house this afternoon

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion I asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Helly-er) what action the government had taken in view of the representations made with regard to the re-routing of the Roberts Bank rail connection. This matter, you will note, Mr. Speaker, has received almost daily attention in this house by way of questions, as well as in our debates, and it is of the utmost concern to those who represent the people of the lower mainland of British Columbia.
The available facts are somewhat meager but it would appear that in 1966 a United States corporation entered into a contract with Japanese interests for the purpose of shipping a substantial quantity of bulk coal from Natal, British Columbia, to Japan. Apparently as a result of negotiations it was agreed that the Canadian Pacific Railway would deliver the coal to a port which the provincial government proposed to construct at Roberts Bank. This arrangement involved the construction of a connecting link between the C.P.R. and the port, and this port was to be constructed by B.C. Hydro, a provincial government authority, financed by the C.P.R.
Early this year the federal government became somewhat apprehensive of the intention of the B.C. government to compete in port facilities on the west coast, and proceeded to construct the port itself under the auspices of the National Harbours Board. About this time concern began to emerge as to the location of the connecting rail link, since it was bound to pass through the lower mainland of British Columbia affecting farm, recreational and urban areas. The chairman of the National Harbours Board is reported in the Vancouver Sun to have stated, quite early on, that all the transport facilities in and out of the port would be channelled in one corridor, and went on to say that the lower mainland regional planning board would be consulted. This board is comprised of representatives of 28 member municipalities and is the principal agency involved in the planning of land use in the lower mainland. This planning has extended to the compilation of a short-range and long-range plan for the whole area.
Oblivious of all planning and totally devoid of any contact with the board, the railway chose a route which was completely unacceptable to any of the member municipalities, effectively destroying much of the farmland involved and certainly adversely affecting the recreational areas of that part of the province.
October 3, 1968

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
This route could easily have been accommodated immediately to the north, where this devastating situation would not have taken place. The inference remains to this date that the decision was made entirely on the basis of what is good for the C.P.R. is good for the nation. As a result of a multiplicity of complaints, the north mainland planning board held a meeting to which all parties were invited, including the officials of the railways, but no one from the railways even condescended to appear to offer any explanation whatsoever concerning the reason for this route. An overwhelming number of briefs was presented at this meeting totally condemning the chosen route.
The question having been raised in the house, the minister has now taken the regrettable position that the federal government seemingly cannot control the actions of even the federal railway that is involved in this ridiculous mistake. It comes as a surprising shock that this link is not to be declared a work for the general benefit of Canada, in that eventually bulk shipments will proceed over this line from the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. It would appear that the ultimate control of that connecting link will come under the aegis of the provincial authorities and not under the aegis of the federal government, where it should be.
It is equally surprising that the C.P.R. cannot be legislated against in order to prohibit actions of this kind that are so deplorably detrimental to the public interest, and to the interest of the people of British Columbia. It is my respectful suggestion that every available resource of the federal government should be brought to bear to prevent this gross travesty that will go down in history as a classic mistake in urban planning. We are paying dearly for some that have been made many years ago in our province as well as in many other provinces of Canada.
The urgency of this matter arises out of the fact that the commencement date for the construction of this railway is obviously imminent, if the coal delivery dates as published in the press are to be relied upon. My question simply is, what action has been taken to give effect to the representations that have been made concerning the rerouting of this line in a more acceptable and viable location.

maintopic: HARBOURS-ROBERTS BANK, B.C.-REPRESENTATIONS RESPECTING RAIL LINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am of course interested in the intervention that has just been made by the hon. member. He has, I think quite rightly, said in summary that the problem here is primarily one of land use and urban planning. As a learned lawyer he is well aware that this is a matter which under our constitution comes solely within the competence of the government of British Columbia, as does the railway which is being built to connect to the port.
Following the representations from members, including those of the hon. members for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Goode) and Fraser Valley East (Mr. Pringle), as well as from the lower mainland regional planning board, and based upon their request for information on the reasons for the decisions of the railways to locate the line on the proposed route, I have written to the railways involved in servicing Roberts Bank, and to the premier of British Columbia, to ask that the railways meet with the executive of the planning board to make known the economic and other considerations which dictated the selection of this railway route. Because of the urgency of the situation, I have asked that this meeting be convened at the earliest possible date.
Motion agreed to and the house adjourned at 10.25 p.m.
